lead: A magnetic circuit is a path built to carry magnetic flux, usually through iron. A coil current creates a magnetomotive force (MMF) that drives flux around the path, while reluctance opposes it. The relation is the same as Ohm's law: flux equals MMF divided by reluctance. This idea explains why a small air gap can control the flux in an inductor, relay or motor, and it gives a quick way to estimate flux before using field software. The chapter builds the quantities, the analogy and one series calculation.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for Ohm's law and series resistance, which make the magnetic-circuit analogy easy to see.

blocks.text: A magnetic circuit is a closed path that carries magnetic flux, usually through iron. Flux Φ is the total magnetic field through a cross-section, measured in weber (Wb). Flux density B is flux per unit area: B = Φ/A, in tesla (T), with A in square metres. For a uniform core, B is the same over the cross-section.

The source is a coil. A current I through N turns produces magnetomotive force F = N I, measured in ampere-turns (A·t). MMF is the driving pressure that pushes flux around the path. The right-hand grip rule gives its direction.

We assume no leakage: all flux stays inside the core. Real cores leak a little, especially at joints. Iron is used because its high permeability guides flux with little MMF. Transformers and motors depend on this guided flux; see transformers and DC machines.
Reluctance S is the opposition to flux. For a uniform part of the path:

blocks.where: l is the path length in metres; A is the cross-section area in square metres; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m is the permeability of free space; μᵣ is the relative permeability (1 for air, thousands for iron); S is in ampere-turns per weber (A·t/Wb). Turns are dimensionless, so A/Wb is the same unit.

blocks.text: Permeability μ = μ₀ μᵣ tells how easily a material carries flux. The magnetic form of Ohm's law is:
Φ = F / S = N I / S
blocks.where: Φ is flux in Wb; F is MMF in A·t; S is reluctance in A·t/Wb; N is turns; I is current in A.

blocks.text: Series parts carry the same flux, so their reluctances add: S_total = S₁ + S₂ + ... . Parallel paths share the same MMF, so 1/S_eq = 1/S₁ + 1/S₂ + ... . Some syllabi call reluctance magnetic resistance and MMF magnetising force; standard books reserve magnetising force for H = F/l, in A/m.
The analogy is a calculation aid, not a full model. Iron saturates, so μᵣ falls at high B, and leakage breaks the simple picture.

sections.h3: The air gap controls the flux

blocks.text: Put an iron core and an air gap in series. The same flux Φ passes both. MMF divides: F_iron = Φ S_iron, F_gap = Φ S_gap, and total F = Φ(S_iron + S_gap). Air has μᵣ = 1 while iron may have μᵣ = 2000 or more, so a short gap can have larger reluctance than a long iron path. In the worked example, 1 mm of air is about four times as reluctant as 50 cm of iron.
Design consequence: the air gap controls flux. Machines keep it as small as mechanical clearance allows. A relay or loudspeaker uses a gap where movement is wanted.

For a core with a central limb, flux splits into parallel limbs. Reluctances combine as parallel resistances. Flux takes the easier path: more flux goes through the limb with lower reluctance, in inverse ratio.

Assumptions: no leakage, no fringing at the gap, uniform area. Fringing makes the effective gap area larger, so real gap reluctance is a little lower. Saturation reduces μᵣ at high flux. A changing flux links later work on Faraday's laws and inductance.

figure.caption: MMF from the coil pushes flux through the iron and then the air gap. The gap reluctance is about four times the iron reluctance, so the gap sets the flux.

spec.title: Series magnetic circuit
spec.aria: A coil produces MMF, which pushes flux through the iron reluctance and then the much larger air-gap reluctance to give 0.161 mWb of flux.

examples.question: An iron ring of mean length 50 cm and cross-section 4 cm² has a 1 mm air gap cut in it. The relative permeability of the iron is 2000 and the coil has 400 turns carrying 1 A. Find the reluctance of the iron, the reluctance of the air gap, the total reluctance, the flux and the flux density. Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
steps: Convert units: l_iron = 50 cm = 0.50 m; l_gap = 1 mm = 1 × 10⁻³ m; A = 4 cm² = 4 × 10⁻⁴ m².
Find permeability: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ H/m. For iron, μ = μ₀ μᵣ = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ × 2000 = 2.513 × 10⁻³ H/m. For air, μ = μ₀.
Total reluctance: S_total = S_iron + S_gap = 4.97359 × 10⁵ + 1.98944 × 10⁶ = 2.48680 × 10⁶ A·t/Wb.
examples.answer: S_iron = 4.97 × 10⁵ A·t/Wb, S_gap = 1.99 × 10⁶ A·t/Wb, S_total = 2.49 × 10⁶ A·t/Wb, Φ = 0.161 mWb and B = 0.40 T.
examples.check:
import math
mu0 = 4 * math.pi * 1e-7
N = 400
I = 1.0
A = 4e-4
l_i = 0.5
l_g = 1e-3
mur = 2000
S_i = l_i / (mu0 * mur * A)
S_g = l_g / (mu0 * 1 * A)
S_t = S_i + S_g
F = N * I
phi = F / S_t
B = phi / A
print(round(S_i, 0))
print(round(S_g, 0))
print(round(S_t, 0))
print(round(phi, 8))
print(round(B, 4))

traps: Using μᵣ = 2000 for the air gap. Air has μᵣ = 1; the gap reluctance comes from μ₀ alone.
Leaving length in cm and area in cm². Convert to metres and square metres before dividing; otherwise the answer moves by powers of ten.
Treating MMF N I and magnetising force H = N I / l as the same. MMF is total ampere-turns; H is ampere-turns per metre.

In a series circuit the same flux passes every part, so the part MMFs are not known until the flux is found. Do not try to add part MMFs first; find S_total, then Φ = F/S_total, then F_iron = ΦS_iron and F_gap = ΦS_gap.
For parallel limbs, adding reluctances as if they were in series. Use reciprocals: 1/S_eq = 1/S₁ + 1/S₂.

quiz.q: Define flux, flux density and MMF, and give their units.
quiz.a: Flux Φ is the total magnetic field, in Wb. Flux density B = Φ/A, in T. MMF F = N I, in A·t.

quiz.q: Why does an iron core carry flux better than air for the same length and area?
quiz.a: Iron has much higher μᵣ, so its reluctance S = l/(μ₀ μᵣ A) is much lower. The same MMF then gives more flux.

quiz.q: A coil of 500 turns carries 0.8 A. The core reluctance is 2.5 × 10⁵ A·t/Wb. Find the flux.
An air gap is 0.5 mm long and has area 6 cm². Find its reluctance. Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
In a series iron core and air gap, which part needs the larger MMF, and why?
quiz.a: The part with larger reluctance needs more MMF, because F = ΦS and the flux is the same. Even a short gap can win because air has μᵣ = 1.

quiz.q: A core has two equal parallel limbs, and one limb contains an air gap. How does the total flux divide?
quiz.a: The gapped limb has higher reluctance, so it takes less flux. Flux divides inversely with reluctance: Φ₁/Φ₂ = S₂/S₁.

quiz.q: Write the magnetic-circuit analogy for EMF, current, resistance and Ohm's law.
quiz.a: EMF ↔ MMF, current ↔ flux, resistance ↔ reluctance, so I = V/R becomes Φ = F/S. Series resistances add, and series reluctances add.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design offices solve reluctance networks with finite-element software that also models fringing and saturation. Electric-vehicle traction motors push the air gap small and the iron close to saturation to get torque from limited volume. Magnetic sensors and wireless power pads use the same MMF-flux-reluctance thinking. Search next for 'magnetic equivalent circuit' and 'fringing flux'.
